Investment memo · Hilton Food Group (HFG-GB) · 3 November 2026

Hilton Food Group: the repair is done and priced, FY2027 probably brings a consensus cut, and the earnings step-up and a fair return at 12x to 14x arrive from FY2028

Written 3 November 2026 at a share price of 715.5p; market value about £650m. Money is in pounds sterling and per-share figures are in pence. The definitions of operating profit and EPS, the consensus source and the two forecast sets used here are set out in the end notes.

#0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

Hilton Food Group is a £0.77bn value-added contract packer inside a £4.6bn-revenue company. Hilton buys about £3.4bn of meat a year on its customers' behalf and passes that cost straight through. Hilton earns its profit, about 18p per kilogram or about £95m a year, for packing 530,000 tonnes in dedicated, automated plants co-located with the leading grocer in each of ten countries. Hilton's revenue therefore tracks cattle prices, while profit per kilogram and tonnes packed are the measures of the business itself.

Seven conclusions matter for the investment decision.

1Repair
done and priced

Hilton's repair is real, executed and already paid for by the market. In ten months a new chief executive (Mark Allen), a new chair and two new regional operating chiefs have sold three non-core units at fair prices, ring-fenced seafood, rewritten the capital framework, refinanced to 2031 and committed capital to three new countries. The shares have risen 60 percent, from January's 447.7p low to 715.5p, and the two-year-forward P/E has risen from 8.1x to 11.75x, which is its five-year median. The market has not yet paid for growth, because no growth has arrived: FY2026 profit falls 3 to 10 percent like-for-like even after the September 2026 guidance raise, which management itself called "technical".

2Earnings path
flat, then up

Hilton's EPS is flat for a year and then steps up. The model has EPS of 57p, 56p, 62p, 69p and 76p for FY2026 to FY2030. FY2027 EPS is flat because three costs land in the same year: the new Canadian plant carries its fixed cost before its volume (£0.5m of profit for the year, after a first-half loss); the finance charge rises by about £3.5m (capitalised interest ends, Bank Rate rises and net debt peaks at about £204m); and the April 2027 wage increase arrives before the open-book reset recovers it. The FY2028 to FY2030 step-up, EPS growth of 10 to 11 percent a year, comes 40 percent from new plants (Canada, Poland and NADEC in Saudi Arabia), 30 percent from removing losses and overheads (seafood and the "One Hilton" programme) and 30 percent from the existing estate growing at about its volume rate.

3Near-term skew
negative

The near-term skew of expectations is negative, not positive. Consensus FY2027 EPS of 57.6p (+9.9 percent) sits above two of the three visible brokers (54.0p, 54.9p and 59.8p) and about 4 percent above our view. Hilton's management sets a low bar and labels its own raises "technical". The probable sequence is a confirmation of guidance in January 2027, a small FY2026 beat in April 2027 driven by the guided 28 percent tax rate, and a FY2027 guidance range whose midpoint is at or below consensus, followed by a 3 to 6 percent cut to FY2027 consensus led by Deutsche Bank. That sequence is the opposite of the "conservative guidance, upgrades ahead" setup Richard looks for. The years that are under-forecast are FY2029 and beyond, which only one broker covers and in which Canada and Poland are not yet ramped. The unpriced positive is Canada's contract: the evidence now indicates that Walmart shares cost overruns and that the fee covers the lease, which would lift Canada's mature operating profit from our £7.5m towards £10m to £15m.

4Business model
caps and gears

Hilton's business model caps the upside and gears the downside. Open-book resets return efficiency gains to the customer, so profit per kilogram on the existing estate is pinned at 18.5p to 19.2p; Hilton has no pricing power at all (the earlier research scored it 12 out of 100). Below operating profit, a finance charge that absorbs 28 percent of operating profit and a 28.5 percent tax rate roughly double the EPS effect of any operating miss. A 1p per kilogram change on the existing estate is worth £5.3m of operating profit, about 4p or 7 to 8 percent of EPS; 1 percent of volume is worth £3.5m to £5m. The range of plausible FY2027 EPS outcomes is about 47p to 61p around a central 55p. That range is wide for a consumer staple and skewed down, because volume losses hit profit within the year while recoveries arrive only at the next annual reset.

5Contracts
the robustness

Hilton's contracts are the source of its robustness, and they are stronger than the earlier research thought. Woolworths runs to 2033, Tesco was extended in early 2026, and the Dutch and Danish renewals were completed in 2025. The probability of losing a material anchor contract within three years is about 3 to 5 percent. The live structural threat is partial: retailers are moving individual product streams to integrated processors that own cattle. Tesco moved its Scottish beef to Foyle and Kepak in H1 FY26, Tesco runs £92m a year of Sustainable Beef Group contracts, and the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is reviewing the ABP and Dovecote Park combination. The model carries this threat as a loss of about 1 percent of West volume a year.

6Fair multiple
12x to 14x, not 20.64x

The dashboard's guideline fair multiple of 20.64x belongs to a different company. The 20.64x figure is the 80th percentile of ten years of Hilton's own valuation history, most of which was the 2010s, when Hilton compounded by following grocers into new countries and traded at 17x to 20x. The last five years hold two profit warnings, a failed diversification into seafood and vegan food, and a P/E range of 8.1x to 18.1x with a median of 11.9x. My fair multiple for a stock that is turning up but whose thesis is not yet proven is 12x to 14x (the five-year median to the five-year 75th percentile). The fair multiple rises to the ten-year "conservative" band of about 15x only if Canada proves in 2028 that Hilton's model still travels. At 13x the return to December 2027 is about 30 percent (earnings 12 percent, multiple 11 percent, dividends 8 percent), not the model's 104 percent; at an unchanged multiple the return is about 20 percent; at a trough 9.5x the return is about nil.

7Lifecycle
turning up

Hilton is turning up in its lifecycle, not broadening. The dashboard's rule says "Broadening" because price and revisions have momentum, but the fundamentals show a thesis that has not yet broadened beyond the repair. Three dated tests decide whether the thesis broadens: the January 2027 trading update (Christmas volumes, and Canada commissioned on time); the 7 April 2027 results (FY2026 delivery and the first FY2027 guidance range); and the September 2027 interim results (H1 FY27, which our base case has flat on profit before tax while consensus implies growth). If Hilton passes all three tests in 2027, the stock is broadening in 2028 with Canada visibly adding to EPS; if Hilton fails the September test, the stock stalls.

Implication for Richard: the risk/reward is not unusually skewed to the positive over the next 12 months, but becomes positive over 18 to 36 months. Hilton is a medium-quality, low-cyclicality business whose cause for concern has largely cleared and whose multiple has already returned to its five-year normal. The remaining case is a modest, back-loaded earnings step-up (EPS +33 percent from FY2026 to FY2030 on the model), paid for with a 4.9 percent dividend yield while waiting. The price of waiting is a 2027 in which consensus probably comes down before the step-up shows. The upside that would make Hilton more than a modest compounder (Canada reaching its return hurdle, a second Walmart site, a capital return once leverage reaches its 1.0x floor) is real but undated, and it sits in 2028 to 2030. The skew is slightly negative over the next 6 to 12 months and positive over 18 to 36 months, so the three dated 2027 tests are the points at which the risk/reward changes.

Next 6 to 12 monthsSlightly negative: consensus probably comes down first
18 to 36 monthsPositive: Canada, Poland and a falling finance charge

Scorecard: the twelve topics

The key judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic

Five operating judgements and one valuation judgement decide what Hilton's shares are worth. The four building blocks below convert each judgement into pence of EPS and pence of share price.

1. Canada's ramp and contract terms: the largest swing, in both directions

BaseCanada earns £0.5m of operating profit in FY2027 (a first-half loss, then a second-half profit), rising to £7.5m by FY2030, on sales rising from £65m to £150m.

BearIf the launch slips past March 2027, or the plant loses money through the second half, Canada's FY2027 operating profit is -£3m. That outcome is a swing of -£3.5m against the base case, about -2.8p of EPS (-5 percent).

BullIf Canada reaches Shore Capital's £1.5m or better, the gain is +£1m of operating profit, or +0.8p of EPS.

The longer-term upside is in the contract terms. Shore Capital's description of the contract, together with the statement that Walmart shares cost overruns, suggests that Canada's fee covers the plant's lease and capital cost. If so, Canada's mature operating profit would be £10m to £15m rather than £7.5m, adding £2.5m to £7.5m by FY2030. That addition is worth +2p to +6p of EPS (+3 to +8 percent on a 76p base), and 26p to 78p a share at 13x. No consensus forecast beyond FY2028 carries this upside.

2. Existing-estate profit per kilogram and West volume: the structural judgement

BaseProfit per kilogram on the existing estate rises from 18.5p to 19.2p, and West volume grows 1 percent a year after a 1 percent annual allowance for streams that retailers re-allocate to other suppliers.

BearIf a further stream of the Scottish-beef kind moves (about 2 percent of West volume, worth £2m to £4m of profit), EPS falls 1.6p to 3.2p (-3 to -6 percent). If the FY2027 reset recovers less of the 2025 to 2026 conversion-cost inflation than the £1m to £2m assumed, or if Ireland's retail price war widens, each 0.5p per kilogram on the West's 280,000 tonnes costs £1.4m of operating profit, about 1.1p of EPS.

The signal that the fee itself is under pressure would be an Oceania margin below 3.0 percent, which the earlier research named as its thesis-breaker. That threshold is not close today; the only reported figure, about 2.45 percent, is measured on an East basis that includes Central Europe and is not directly comparable. A 1p per kilogram fall across the whole group would cost 4.2p of EPS (7.5 percent).

3. Australian cattle availability in 2027 and 2028: the external judgement

BaseThe model carries a probability-weighted £1.5m drag on East operating profit in FY2028, against Meat & Livestock Australia (MLA) projections of cattle slaughter falling 6 percent in 2027 and 9 percent in 2028.

BearA full volume effect would be larger. Hilton packs about 190,000 tonnes a year in Australasia, so 1 percent of that volume is about 1,900 tonnes. On a fixed plant base each lost kilogram costs about £0.70 to £0.95 of contribution (value added of £1.47 per kilogram, less the variable part of conversion cost), so each percentage point of lost volume costs about £1.3m to £1.8m. A 3 percent volume fall would cost about £4m to £5m in FY2028, roughly 3p to 4p of EPS (-5 to -7 percent), against the £1.5m in the base case.

Hilton's fee per kilogram protects the cash earned on each kilogram, not the number of kilograms. Hilton's percentage margin falls mechanically whenever beef prices rise, so the percentage margin says nothing about the health of the business.

4. The finance charge and the tax rate: the gearing judgement below operating profit

BaseNet financial items peak at £30.0m in FY2027 (the full path is in topic #5); the tax rate is 28.0 percent in FY2026 and 28.5 percent thereafter.

RatesA Bank Rate 50 basis points above the assumed path costs about £2.1m, about 1.7p of EPS (3 percent). A rate reversal in 2027, which is Rothschild Redburn's view, would add the same amount.

TaxEach point of tax rate is worth 0.8p to 1.0p of EPS (1.4 percent). Consensus assumes a tax rate of about 29.7 percent for FY2026 against the company's guided 28 percent; that gap is worth about 1.3p and is the cleanest source of a FY2026 beat. For FY2028 consensus assumes 27.8 percent against our 28.5 percent, a gap worth -0.6p.

5. Foppen: the binary judgement

BaseThe seafood division moves from -£3.5m to +£1.0m of operating profit by FY2030. The odds are even that Foppen, the seafood business whose Greek plant is barred from the United States, is either re-approved or sold by 2027 to 2028.

Re-approvalRe-approval would add about £3m to £4m of adjusted operating profit (+2.4p to +3.2p of EPS) and £10m to £15m a year of cash, as production inefficiency and exceptional costs end.

SaleA distressed sale would deliver the same adjusted gain and stop the cash drain, but would write down Foppen's goodwill (£18.3m) and intangible assets (£18.6m) in statutory profit.

RestrictionContinued restriction through 2027 would cost £1m against the base case, and the exceptional cash outflow would continue.

Foppen's effect on adjusted EPS is therefore small, while its effect on cash and statutory profit is not.

The multiple is the judgement that dominates the return. Moving from today's 11.75x to 13x adds 11 percent to the price; moving to 15x adds 28 percent; moving to the guideline 20.64x adds 76 percent; falling to a trough 9.5x takes 19 percent off. Each of these moves outweighs any single operating judgement above, which is why the fair multiple (topic #11) matters more than any other topic in this memo.

#1Tailwinds in the operating environment, and the absence of headwinds

Conclusion: the external environment supplies Hilton's new business and taxes its existing business; the environment is a ceiling on earnings, not a floor, with a net effect that is mildly negative over 18 months and neutral over three years.

One strong, durable tailwind supports Hilton: grocers are moving own-label protein and fresh prepared food to a few scaled contract makers on long contracts. That tailwind delivered Walmart Canada, NADEC in Saudi Arabia and Żabka's business in Romania. The disruption that once threatened a red-meat packer, plant-based protein, has been disproved, and weight-loss drugs favour protein. The Australian dollar has also been a currency-translation tailwind this year.

The headwinds are larger in the near term, and the largest is a tightening beef supply to 2028. Hilton's cost-plus contracts turn beef inflation into revenue rather than lost margin, but beef inflation still leaks into Hilton's profit through four channels:

  • an annual lag in repricing conversion costs;
  • consumer trade-down from steak to mince and to lighter packs, which cut West core meat profit by 20.5 percent in H1 FY26 even though volume rose 0.6 percent;
  • interest on about £150m of working-capital finance that customers provide;
  • retailers' growing preference for suppliers that own their own cattle.

Rising UK labour costs (the National Living Wage and National Insurance) are passed through to customers with a lag of up to a year. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) still bars Foppen's Greek plant from its best market, the United States, after every date the company has given for re-approval. The UK consumer is weaker after the 28 October 2026 Budget.

Inference: the tailwind and the headwinds act on different parts of the business and on different timescales. The tailwind acts on contract wins and new countries, which arrive one at a time and need Hilton's own capital. The headwinds act now, on profit per kilogram and on West volume. The net effect caps operating profit growth on the existing estate at mid-single digits, and it makes FY2027 to FY2028 resemble the stress years (FY2022 and FY2025) in which Hilton has historically missed its forecasts.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side reads Hilton's cost-plus model as insulation from the environment and stops there. The sell-side does not model Australian cattle as a volume risk (that analysis sits in Morgan Stanley's protein research and in Woolworths' coverage, not in Hilton's coverage), and it does not connect Tesco's integration moves to Hilton. I think the environment is mildly negative for FY2027 earnings and neutral over three years; the market's narrative treats the environment as neutral-to-positive now.

Counter-case. European beef prices could plateau (pork oversupply and consumers' price sensitivity would cap them); Australian retailers could hold volume by absorbing part of the price rise (retailers passed through only 50 to 60 percent of past rises); and a defensive rotation into staples could lift the shares. What would change my view: Woolworths' quarterly fresh-food volumes holding up through 2027, and Meat & Livestock Australia softening its slaughter projections.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. The one structural tailwind (grocers outsourcing own-label protein to a few scaled packers, which delivered Walmart Canada, NADEC and Romania) is durable but arrives one contract at a time, while beef supply tightening to 2028, Australian cattle availability falling from 2027, consumer trade-down (West core meat profit -20.5% on +0.6% volume), retailer integration with processors and the FDA hold on Foppen tax profit per kilogram now; consensus sales growth at the 30th percentile is a fair read once price pass-through is stripped out. Net mildly negative over 18 months and neutral over three years, coherent with the group's 42: just below Carlsberg's modest mature environment and above Fevertree's flat market with levies.

#2Internally driven corporate change, and the absence of problems

Conclusion: Hilton's internal change is strong, broad, credible and already executed, but it repairs a business whose economics the change cannot alter. The change therefore produces 8 to 10 percent EPS growth from a trough rather than a higher trajectory, and the market has already paid for the repair.

Hilton's internal change is complete at every level, and it took under ten months. Steve Murrells left as chief executive in November 2025. Mark Allen, who spent twelve years at Dairy Crest up to its £1.21bn sale, became Executive Chair and then Group Chief Executive from 1 July 2026, and he bought 42,500 shares at 468p, near the low. Mark Clare became independent Chair, the Audit and Remuneration Committees have new chairs, two regional Chief Operating Officers have arrived (Samy Zekhout from Nomad Foods for the West, Melanie Chambers for the East), and a full-time Investor Relations Director has been appointed. The new team has sold three non-core units at fair prices, ring-fenced seafood under a review of "all options", and committed capital to three new countries.

A new capital framework (March 2026) and a £450m bank facility running to 2031 complete the financial reset. The framework's targets are set out below.

Inference: on its inputs, Hilton's corporate change is among the broadest in the universe; on its outputs, the change is modest. The September 2026 guidance raise already removed Dalco's losses from the FY2026 continuing base. The remaining self-help pool is therefore seafood (about £4.5m) and retained overheads (about £3.5m), and the new countries add only £1m to £3m a year of profit at first. Two internal signals say to model modestly. First, the July 2026 incentive awards vest between 3 percent and 8 percent compound EPS growth, so management is paid in full for the consensus path; the 2023 plan ran from 6.3 to 11.2 percent and vested at only 2.3 percent. Second, FY2026 guidance, even after the raise, is a like-for-like decline.

Beneath the new leadership, five problems remain: weak controls, low executive ownership, recurring "exceptional" cash costs, creeping capital budgets and a record of late projects. Each is set out below.

Where I differ from the market. The market's narrative is "repair done, recovery coming". I agree with the first half. I think the recovery is slower and smaller than the +9.9 percent FY2027 EPS growth in consensus implies, because the lever that produced the September raise (the Dalco exit) does not repeat, and the next lever (Canada) carries fixed cost before it adds profit.

Counter-case. The new team has beaten its own bar once: H1 FY26 profit of £32.8m came in above Shore Capital's £31.5m and Deutsche Bank's £29.0m. The team's honesty also raises the odds that its guidance survives. What would change my view: a disclosed savings target for the "One Hilton" programme, or a Foppen resolution that turns about £15m a year of cash drag into cash.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. A full internal change executed in ten months (new CEO who bought at the low, chair, two regional COOs, three non-core exits at fair prices, seafood ring-fenced, a new capital framework, refinancing to 2031) plus three new countries (Canada, Poland, Saudi), which supply about 70% of the FY2028-30 EPS step-up with seafood loss removal and overheads; net of internal problems (control deficiencies and two restatements, about £10m a year of recurring exceptional cash, capital creep, every recent project late, incentives topping at 8% EPS growth). I weigh the new-country moves a little above the Analyst and the group's 60, because large strategic moves count as large change forces even though the earnings output is back-loaded; above Odfjell's acquisition-and-deleverage case, below OEM's working acquirer with a record quarter.

#3Value chain, business model, financial profile, management

Conclusion: Hilton is a durable, defensible, medium-quality business with a real volume moat and no pricing power, run by a sound repair team with modest ambition. Hilton's structure supports continuity and caps margin, so the fair multiple is a utility's, not a compounder's, until new countries prove otherwise.

Hilton sits in the squeezed middle of a value chain whose two ends are both gaining power. Above Hilton are concentrated grocers; below Hilton are consolidating primary processors constrained by the scarcity of cattle. Hilton owns no animals, feed or slaughter. The grocers' buying power over Hilton is absolute: they audit Hilton's books, track raw-material indices daily, hold benchmarking clauses that allow a re-tender, and can re-allocate product streams inside a partnership, as Tesco did in Scotland. In mature markets the advantaged competitor is the one that owns the animal, such as Cranswick. Hilton is the advantaged independent packer for grocers that want to outsource packing without being tied to a processor's cattle, which is why Walmart and NADEC chose Hilton.

Hilton's moats protect volume and relationships, but none of them protects price. Hilton has one strong moat, customer embedding, and one moderate moat, automation combined with a multi-country execution record. Entering Hilton's business requires a retailer partner and tens of millions of pounds of capital, and there is no spot market to sell into. Hilton's model is built to share scale economies with the customer at every contract reset, so the reset is the source of both the model's durability and its margin cap.

Hilton's financial profile is weak on margin by construction, adequate on returns, volatile on cash and geared on EPS. Hilton earns the lowest margin of its four peers, carries the highest lease-inclusive leverage and is the most concentrated by customer. Hilton's returns are also flattered by about £150m of customer-provided working-capital finance that sits outside debt.

Hilton's management is a competent, decisive repair team with deliberately modest ambition. Mark Allen's record at Dairy Crest is value realised through an exit while organic margins drifted down. The new team has not yet out-executed anybody, but it has done what a repair requires, told the truth about its own upgrade, and bought shares. The organisation beneath the leadership, in its controls and its mid-level depth, is weaker than the leadership itself. The team is neither a Cranswick, which is a capacity-led compounder, nor a Greencore, which has a disclosed synergy target and buys back shares.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side calls Canada a "growth supercharger" and leaves the open-book reset unstated; Deutsche Bank, for example, holds Hilton's margin flat for a decade without saying why. I think the open-book reset is the most important fact about the business. The reset explains why automation is defensive rather than margin-enhancing, why the 2010s multiple is gone, and why new countries are Hilton's only route to growth.

Counter-case. Hilton's contracts are long and were all renewed; primary processors cannot quickly replicate automated, co-located plants; and the model survived 30 to 50 percent beef inflation with volumes up. What would change my view: a contract (Canada's may be one) that lets Hilton keep its efficiency gains for the contract's term, or a visible rise in the fee per kilogram at a renewal.

Score: 41, set by the Rater. A real volume moat (co-located automated plants, 5-15 year contracts, none lost, Woolworths to 2033) sits inside a squeezed-middle value chain with absolute buyer power, no pricing power by construction and five customers for nearly all revenue; management is a sound repair team with modest ambition over weak controls and a thin bench. The figures confirm it: operating margin at the 6th percentile and EBITDA margin at the 4th, return on invested capital 6.4% (47th) with return on capital employed near 20% flattered by about £150m of customer finance, negative free cash flow (9.6th), new capital earning 15-20% pre-tax only if Canada hits its hurdle, and two warnings in five years cutting predictability; coherent with the groups (38, 45, 32, 50), between IMCD's real moat with weak returns and Teqnion's sub-par returns on acquired capital.

#4Conservatism of guidance, sell-side management, and the record of upgrades

Conclusion: FY2026 guidance is mildly conservative and largely priced; the mid-term framework is fair rather than conservative; and Hilton is an honest tracker of its numbers, not an upgrader, so the probability of guidance-led upgrades over the next 12 months is low.

Hilton's FY2026 profit guidance has moved from two cuts to one "technical" raise. Guidance for FY2026 adjusted profit before tax was set at £60m to £65m in January 2026 after two cuts, held in March and May, and raised by 9.5 percent at the midpoint, to £66m to £71m, in September 2026. The September raise came from excluding Dalco's losses (about £3.7m) and from Australian-dollar translation. Shore Capital called the raise "a technical adjustment rather than operational surge", and management did not disagree. The new midpoint (£68.5m) sits about 1 percent above consensus (£67.9m), and the top of the range is above every broker's forecast.

Hilton guides little beyond profit before tax and tax. The company guides a tax rate of about 28 percent (H1 FY26 was 27.7 percent), while consensus EPS implies about 29.7 percent. The mid-term framework (mid-single-digit operating profit growth on average, excluding seafood, and not necessarily linear) is the same growth rate as the 2023 framework, applied to a narrower business. Hilton gives no guidance on volume, margin, finance costs or Canada's profit.

Hilton's record is two profit warnings in five years, both in inflation spikes. The warnings came in FY2022 and Q3 FY2025, the latter causing a 23 percent one-day fall in the shares. Hilton has delivered in stable years, and it has beaten once, against a bar that had been reset lower.

Inference: FY2026 guidance is mildly conservative, so the upper half of the range is more likely than the lower half. The £66m to £71m range implies second-half profit before tax of £33.2m to £38.2m, against about £38m a year earlier, and the second half has three named tailwinds: the Australian dollar, the end of airfreight costs and Seachill's cost reductions. Our expectation is therefore £69m to £70m, which at a 28 percent tax rate gives about 54p of EPS against consensus's 52.4p. The mid-term framework is fair rather than conservative once Australian cattle and retailer pressure are netted against the new countries. Hilton is not an upgrader: it has made one technical raise against two cuts in two years. The new team's behaviour is honest tracking, which raises the reliability of what the team says and lowers the odds of a "beat and raise" habit.

Where I differ from the market. The market has already priced the upper half of FY2026 guidance, because the shares re-rated on the September raise. I expect FY2027 guidance in April 2027 to be set at or just below consensus. The arithmetic is that "mid-single-digit growth excluding seafood" on a FY2026 operating profit base of about £99m gives about £102m to £104m of operating profit, and about £72m to £73m of profit before tax after a £30m finance charge, against consensus's £74.0m. The sell-side at Hilton follows guidance rather than leading it: Shore Capital matched the January 2026 cut within days.

Counter-case. Management's informal commentary runs slightly ahead of its formal numbers (the core business is "structurally strong", Poland is "bigger than envisaged" and Canada is "a significant driver of future earnings"), and a Foppen resolution would produce a genuine raise. What would change my view: a January 2027 statement pointing to the top of the FY2026 range, with Canada commissioned on time.

Score: 37, set by the Rater. The two-to-three-year record weighs heavily: a 23% one-day profit warning in Q3 FY2025, cuts in November 2025 and January 2026, then one H1 beat against a reset bar and a September raise that Shore Capital called technical (Dalco exclusion and currency); current FY2026 guidance is mildly conservative and largely priced, the mid-term framework is fair rather than conservative, and FY2027 guidance is more likely to land below consensus than above. Slightly below the groups (48 and 42) because the misses are recent; below Fevertree, whose cuts were in 2022-23, and above Solid State's warnings with a revenue collapse.

#5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops

Conclusion: revenue growth does not lead to outsized profit growth in Hilton's existing estate, because the reset returns efficiency gains to the customer and the finance charge gears any miss. The only place where Hilton's growth compounds is a new dedicated plant filling up under a fixed fee, which is why Canada carries the case.

Hilton has no pricing power. Over 90 percent of raw-material cost passes through on indices within ten to twelve weeks; conversion costs reset annually under the UK open-book model; the fee is set by audit and benchmarking; and retailers "actively resist real-time price pass-throughs". Price added about 7 points to FY2026 revenue growth and nothing to profit, so price is a revenue line for Hilton and dilutes the percentage margin whenever prices rise. The only price mechanism that touches profit is the lagged recovery of conversion-cost inflation (about £1m to £2m in FY2027), and the reset that recovers that inflation also re-benchmarks the fee.

Hilton's operating leverage is material against volume, nil against revenue, and asymmetric in time. A large part of Hilton's conversion cost is fixed within a year, so volume moves operating profit sharply. Volume losses hit profit in the half in which they occur: Seachill turned loss-making on a 6.8 percent volume fall, and West core meat profit fell 20.5 percent when the Scottish stream moved. Efficiency gains, by contrast, are shared back with the customer at the next reset. The favourable operating leverage that Hilton keeps is in new dedicated plants. Canada's incremental margin on sales growth is about four times the group's, because the fee is fixed for a ten-year term and the fixed cost is already in place. New plants therefore supply most of the FY2028 to FY2030 increase in operating profit.

Hilton's financial leverage is neutral in FY2027 and favourable from FY2028. In FY2027 the finance charge rises to about £30m: about £3.2m a year of capitalised interest returns to the income statement when the Brantford plant in Canada starts, Bank Rate reaches about 4.25 percent by mid-2027, and net bank debt peaks. The rising charge turns operating profit growth of about 6 percent into profit-before-tax growth of about 3 percent. From FY2028 the charge stops rising and then falls as net bank debt comes down, adding 2 to 3 points a year to profit-before-tax growth. Interest cover rises from 3.6x to 4.6x, and covenant headroom is ample. Including £198m of leases, FactSet's net debt is about £390m; the lease figure rises by about £60m, with no cash effect, when the Canadian building lease is recognised in 2027. About £150m of customer-provided finance sits outside both measures.

Hilton's cost-out adds about £8m to £9m of retained profit by FY2030, and most of it arrives late. Removing seafood losses adds about £4.5m; "One Hilton" overhead savings add about £3.5m, although Hilton has disclosed no target and the predecessor programme was re-phased; and automation is a £1m to £2m float that is returned to customers at resets. The larger cost benefit, about £15m a year less exceptional cash by FY2029, reaches free cash flow and statutory profit but not adjusted EPS.

Hilton's feedback loops make profit per kilogram mean-reverting and volume step-wise. The dominant loop is the open-book reset, which pins the existing estate's profit per kilogram. The one reinforcing positive loop, in which a partnership record wins the next partner, is real but slow and lumpy. The next step of that positive loop, a second Walmart site, has no date, site or budget, and Walmart's habit in the United States is to own its case-ready plants (Thomasville in 2020, Olathe in 2025).

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side treats Hilton's cost-plus model as a margin protector. The sell-side does not model the reset as a cap on margin, and it does not model the end of capitalised interest or the interest-rate path. I think the market's long-run margin expectation for Hilton is above both the earlier research's and mine.

Score: 33, set by the Rater. Pricing power is nil (over 90% of raw material passed through, conversion costs reset annually, the fee set by audit and benchmarking), and the 40-60% of conversion cost that is fixed gears volume losses within the half while efficiency gains are returned at the next reset, so operating leverage is asymmetric and works against the company on the way down; a finance charge of about 28% of operating profit doubles the EPS effect of a miss, cost-out is only £8-9m and late, and the loops are balancing apart from the slow, lumpy partner-to-partner win. The forecast EPS-to-revenue growth ratio of about 1.9x is near the median only because of new fixed-fee plants and a falling finance charge from FY2028, so between the 25 and 50 levels and coherent with the groups (32 and 40).

#6Forecast financials and scope for double-digit growth

Conclusion: the forecasts describe a slow, back-loaded recovery, with FY2027 EPS flat and double-digit EPS growth only in FY2028 to FY2030. The recovery is built on two new plants and on loss removal rather than on a better existing business. The model's shape is more credible than consensus's, and the model's quantum is similar to consensus's by FY2028.

The model's forecasts show EPS flat in FY2027, then rising 10 to 11 percent a year, while cash turns from a deficit to a strong surplus. FY2026 revenue of £4,618m is 12.4 percent above the restated £4,108m base, and price and currency supply about 10 points of that growth. IFRS 16 EBITDA rises from £167.6m in FY2026 to £210.0m in FY2030, a margin of 3.6 to 3.9 percent. The model does not yet deduct exceptional cash, so the Analyst deducts it to give strict free cash flow.

Hilton's strict free cash flow does not cover the dividend until FY2028, so the balance sheet funds the dividend in FY2026 and FY2027. Leverage of 1.4x at the FY2027 peak sits comfortably inside the 2.0x ceiling, so that funding is affordable.

Five drivers produce the model's path: tonnes, profit per kilogram on the existing estate, the new plants, seafood and capital expenditure.

Against Hilton's own past, the forecast is a recovery, not a new trajectory. From FY2019 to FY2025 revenue grew 2.3 times on acquisitions and inflation, while FactSet's adjusted EBIT margin halved from 2.7 to 1.4 percent, company EPS fell from 61.0p (FY2024) to 56.0p (FY2025), and free cash flow averaged about nil. The forecast has operating profit growing about 6.7 percent a year and EPS 8 to 9 percent a year from the FY2026 trough, but only 3.4 percent a year from FY2025 to FY2028. EPS regains its FY2024 level only in FY2028, and operating profit returns above FY2024's £104.7m only in FY2029. The real change is in cash: strict free cash flow turns from a £36m deficit in FY2026 to about £60m a year once Canada and Poland are built.

Hilton's EPS grows at double digits only in FY2028 to FY2030, at 10 to 11 percent a year, from a depressed base and with financial gearing turning favourable. EPS does not grow at double digits in FY2027. Over four years Hilton has scope for higher growth than in the past, because new plants add contracted volume that the past acquisitions never did. Hilton has no scope for a higher margin on the existing estate, which stays inside its FY2024 to FY2025 range. The group's profit per kilogram rises from 17.9p to 20.5p only through mix.

Where I differ from the market: consensus has the shape of the EPS path wrong. I am above consensus in FY2026, because of the tax rate and the upper half of guidance; the model's +7.9 percent gap overstates the difference because the model omits minorities, and the like-for-like gap is about +3 percent. I am below consensus in FY2027 by 2 to 4 percent (the finance charge, Canada's start-up and no further Dalco benefit) and in FY2028 by 1 to 3 percent. I am above the single broker in FY2029 by 2 to 4 percent, because Canada and Poland are ramping. Consensus rebounds 9.9 percent in FY2027 partly because it carries FY2025's higher tax rate into FY2026, which depresses the FY2026 base.

Counter-case. Canada at Shore Capital's £1.5m, Foppen re-approved and a firm Australian dollar would together give FY2027 EPS of about 61p to 63p, above consensus. What would change my view: H1 FY27 profit before tax above £35m, reported in September 2027.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The 5-10% band gives C; I place it in the lower-middle of the band because FY2027 is flat and the growth is back-loaded from a trough, the existing estate's margin stays inside its FY2024-25 range (profit per kilogram rises only through mix), and operating profit regains FY2024's level only in FY2029. Against that the growth is organic and contracted (new dedicated plants, loss removal), not bought as the 2019-25 growth was, which keeps it above the bottom of the band.

#7Scope for upgrades to guidance, consensus and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Conclusion: over the next 6 to 12 months the scope is for a small FY2026 upgrade that is already priced and a FY2027 consensus cut of 3 to 6 percent that is not priced. The scope for upgrades lies in FY2029 and beyond, which the market has barely forecast.

FY2026 consensus is more likely to rise than fall, but the market has already paid for that rise. FY2026 consensus EPS of 52.4p has about a 60 percent chance of rising by 2 to 4 percent, on the guided tax rate and the upper half of the guidance range.

FY2027 consensus is too high and rests on a broker that cannot be seen. The FY2027 consensus median of 57.6p rests on an unnamed contributor at or above about 60p; the median of the three visible brokers is 54.9p. No broker models the end of capitalised interest, a higher Bank Rate or Canada's first-half loss. Deutsche Bank's 59.8p includes an uplift for the Dalco exit measured against its own old forecast, rather than against the FY2026 continuing base. The company will probably set FY2027 guidance below consensus (topic #4).

Revisions and targets have recovered only part of the ground lost in 2025. FY2027 EPS consensus has risen 8 percent over three months but is down 18 percent over twelve months. Target prices have risen 17 percent in three months to a mean of 795p, although Peel Hunt's 720p target is at today's price, and every broker rates the shares a Buy.

Inference: the probable 2027 sequence turns sell-side momentum negative before the earnings step-up arrives. The sequence below ends with the dashboard's revision-momentum score (15 today) probably falling below zero by mid-2027, which would cost the stock its pinned B grade for sell-side momentum. The outer years are the reverse: FY2029 consensus rests on one broker at 66.6p, below our 67.7p to 69p, and a second broker adding a FY2029 forecast after Canada commissions would lift that consensus.

The market's narrative about Hilton is thin and incomplete on both sides. Only two brokers (Deutsche Bank and Shore Capital) cover Hilton in depth, no investor commentary was found, and the share register is passive: Aberforth holds 8.6 percent, Vanguard 5.0 percent, Western Standard 5.0 percent (since July 2026), Newtyn trimmed to 4.99 percent in October, and the Heffer family holdings are 4.7 and 3.2 percent. The narrative misses four negatives and three positives.

Where I differ from the market. The market is positioned for 9 to 10 percent FY2027 EPS growth, with unanimous Buy ratings. I think the next two events produce a small FY2026 beat and a reset of FY2027 expectations. The under-modelled upside is dated 2028 to 2029, not 2027: Canada's contract terms, a second broker forecasting FY2029, and a capital return as leverage falls below 1.0x.

Counter-case. A Foppen resolution would be a genuine FY2027 upgrade of 2p to 3p of EPS and a cash story; Deutsche Bank "expects a resolution of some sort", and Shore Capital expects Foppen to stop being a drag by H2 2027. Canada at £1.5m and a firm Australian dollar would also hold consensus up. What would change my view: a January 2027 statement that Canada is commissioned and ramping ahead of plan.

Score: 26, set by the Rater. The likely sequence is a small FY2026 beat already priced (tax rate, upper half of the range) and then a FY2027 range at or below consensus (45% below, 40% in line, 15% above) with a 3-6% cut to FY2027 consensus EPS (57.6p sits above two of three visible brokers and about 4% above the Analyst), which against revenue growth of about 3.7% is a ratio of roughly -0.7 to -1.1, with Foppen the only binary near-term upside and the narrative more likely to cool than improve; the under-forecast FY2029 and Canada's contract terms lie outside the 6-12 month window. Below the group's 36 because the size rule makes a 3-6% cut on low growth weigh heavily; below Indutrade, where downgrades were merely as likely as upgrades, and above Prosus's investment-driven cuts.

#8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and peers

Conclusion: Hilton's momentum is positive on every pinned measure and fragile on every underlying one. The momentum is the reversal of a collapse, not yet a trend, and both the market regime and the April 2027 results lean against it.

Every momentum measure reads positive today.

  • Guidance momentum: one raise (the technical raise of September 2026) after two cuts (November 2025 and January 2026).
  • Sell-side momentum (pinned B): FY2027 EPS revisions of +1 percent over one month, +8 percent over three and six months, and -18 percent over twelve months; target prices up 17 percent in three months; 100 percent of brokers rate the shares a Buy after a 60-point rise in that share in three months.
  • Narrative momentum: positive but thin (The Grocer: "turnaround gathers steam"; Investors Chronicle: "offers hope of a recovery").
  • Technical momentum (pinned B): the price is up 19.4 percent over three months, 33.1 percent over six, 52.3 percent over nine and 10.8 percent over twelve. The price is 25.7 percent above a 200-day average (569p) that has risen in only two of the last twelve months, relative strength is at the 87th percentile of the universe, and the 52-week high is 738p.
  • Co-movement with peers: low. Peers explain 10 percent of Hilton's daily price variance over six months (correlation 0.31, beta 0.74), and the stock returned +35 percent against the food-production basket's +5 percent.
  • The market regime: Consumer staples and Food production are Overweight, but the Momentum factor has been Underweight since 23 October 2026, and Fragility (small companies with multi-part cases) is Double Underweight.

The sector is not carrying Hilton; Hilton is trading on its own news. Cranswick has a technical grade of D, a sell-side grade of B, a P/E of 14.8x (its 11th percentile) and revisions of +13. Greencore has D and B, 9.4x and revisions of +13. LDC has D and C, 10.0x and 100 percent Buy ratings. Cloetta has B and B, and 17.5x at its 93rd percentile.

Inference: Hilton's momentum is strong, early and fragile. The momentum is early because the 200-day average has only just turned up, and the uptrend is only ten months old, measured from a low set after the chief executive had left. The momentum is fragile because a technical guidance upgrade and a reversing de-rating drove the rise, the Buy ratings are unanimous, liquidity is thin (about $2.7m traded a day), and the next catalyst (April 2027) is more likely to reset FY2027 expectations than to raise them. The market regime has turned against exactly this profile of stock.

Where I differ from the market. The pinned B grades are right on the data. I weight them lower than the dashboard's rule does, because the revision series is the reversal of a deep cut rather than a rising trend (the twelve-month revision is still -18 percent), and because I expect revisions to turn down in April 2027.

Counter-case. A defensive rotation could broaden the buying (the July 2026 reading showed Hilton trading as a staple when staples led), and a January 2027 update confirming Canada could extend the uptrend through the spring. What would change my view: the 200-day average rising for six consecutive months, with revisions still positive after the April 2027 results.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. Both measures are in the top fifth and no part is negative: the last guidance move was a raise (technical, after two cuts), FY2027 EPS is +8% over three and six months (about 1.7 times revenue growth), targets +17% and Buys 100%, the narrative is positive if thin, and the price is 25.7% above its 200-day average near its 52-week high; peers are weak but do not pull the letter down. I place it at the floor of A because the 200-day average has only just turned (rising in two of twelve months), the twelve-month revision is still -18% so this is a reversal rather than a trend, and the regime has turned against momentum and fragility.

#9Riskiness and simplicity of forecasts and expectations

Conclusion: Hilton's case is simple and checkable in structure, concentrated in a handful of dated drivers, and geared in effect. The case is moderately-to-highly risky over the next 18 months, because the drivers that can go wrong act fast while the drivers that can go right act slowly, and a fair trough price sits about 20 percent below today's price.

Hilton's case is simple in structure and concentrated in a few drivers, which makes it checkable at dated points. Profit is tonnes times the fee per kilogram, less a finance charge and tax, and every link is visible at results. Six items (Canada, seafood, the existing estate's volume and fee, Poland and NADEC, Australian cattle, and tax and interest) explain almost all of the difference between the forecast and the record. Three of the six (one plant, one regulator and one tax rate) explain most of the EPS difference. The case therefore depends on dated checkpoints rather than on a broad margin assumption.

The forecast needs seven things to go right in FY2027, a year that contains both conditions under which Hilton has missed before. Hilton's record is to slip project dates and to miss in years of raw-material stress.

Hilton's sudden risks are structural, and each one is large in effect, because it acts through a 2 percent margin and a finance charge of 28 percent of operating profit. The risks are listed below.

Hilton's forecasts are hard to track between results. The company reports twice a year and guides none of the forecast's links except tax. Only Australian cattle can be followed monthly from outside, through Meat & Livestock Australia data, the Eastern Young Cattle Indicator and Woolworths' quarterly results.

Hilton's perception risk is above average. The stock is small and illiquid, every broker rates it a Buy, it has risen 60 percent from its low, and it sits on the wrong side of two regime tilts (Momentum and Fragility).

The range of FY2027 outcomes is wide and skewed down. For FY2026 the range is 52.5p to 55.5p of EPS with about 75 percent probability, skewed slightly up against consensus. For FY2027 the range is 47p to 61p around 55p (±13 percent; profit before tax of £60m to £79m), and the mean is about 1p below the central case. The FY2027 range is skewed down because the bear ingredients (Canada late, lower Australian volume, a West stream lost, Foppen unresolved, higher rates) act within the year, while the bull ingredients (Foppen re-approved, Canada faster, currency) either lag or are binary. Statutory EPS has a wider range still, because of £21m of adjusting items in H1 FY26, the IFRS 18 standard, and a Foppen impairment test that a 2.4 percent fall in Foppen's EBITDA would trigger.

Sector precedents show that Hilton fits the outperformance pattern on volume visibility and repair, and the underperformance pattern on inflation spikes. Protein and chilled-food contract makers outperform when visible contracted volume arrives with falling margin volatility (Cranswick's decade; Hilton's own 2010s), or when self-help lifts a troughed margin and returns cash (Greencore from 2023 to 2025). They underperform on acquisitions outside the core (Hilton's seafood and vegan businesses), on inflation spikes that expose pass-through lags (Hilton in 2022 and 2025; Greencore in 2018), and on food-safety shocks that do not pass quickly (Foppen, in contrast to Cranswick's 2022 recall). Hilton fits the outperformance pattern on volume visibility and portfolio repair, but not on margin or cash return. Hilton fits the underperformance pattern on inflation spikes, and the next spike, in Australian beef, is already visible. The Wisdom Library's base rate, "turnarounds take longer than you think", applies to seafood and to Canada's return hurdle.

A fair trough price is about 20 percent below today's price, and a severe trough returns the shares to their 52-week low. The fair trough applies a trough multiple to unchanged earnings; the severe trough applies a lower multiple to trough earnings, with two-year-forward EPS cut 10 percent to about 55p. The 4.9 percent yield softens either trough but does not change it.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's models assume a smooth January launch in Canada and hold the margin flat without modelling the risks around it. I think the FY2027 range of outcomes is wider and more skewed down than a consensus of unanimous Buys implies, and that the tail risk of losing an anchor contract is smaller than the earlier research feared.

Score: 40, set by the Rater. The case is simple in structure (tonnes times fee per kilogram, less interest and tax) and the anchor-contract tail is small (3-5% over three years), but the FY2027 cone is 47p-61p (±13%, wide for a staple and skewed down because bear ingredients act within the year), the sudden risks (a stream re-allocated, a food-safety event, a Canada slip at 20-30% odds) are geared through a 2% margin, a finance charge of 28% of operating profit and lease-inclusive leverage of 3.3x, trackability between half-years is poor, and a small, illiquid, unanimously-Buy stock 60% off its low carries a fair trough about 20% below the price. Coherent with the groups (40 and 45); just above Fevertree's margin-cap and transition risk, below OMV Petrom's sudden fiscal interventions.

#10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Conclusion: Hilton is turning up, about ten months into its recovery, with the repair priced and the growth unproven. Hilton becomes a broadening case only if it passes the January, April and September 2027 checkpoints, which I put at a little better than even odds.

The dashboard's rule says "Broadening", but the evidence says "turning up, with the thesis not yet broadened". The dashboard's reading rests on price momentum (B), revisions (B) and relative strength (87th percentile). A thesis broadens when the growth engine is seen to work beyond the repair, and Hilton's engine (new countries under fixed-fee contracts) first becomes visible in H2 FY27 and first becomes material in FY2028.

The evidence for "turning up" is that the cause for concern has cleared. The profit warning, the chief executive's exit, the guidance cut and the failed diversifications have been addressed in governance, in the group's perimeter and on the balance sheet. Consensus has been cut deeply and has partly recovered.

The evidence against "broadening" is that growth has not yet arrived. FY2026 is a like-for-like decline, the September raise was technical, FY2027 is flat on our numbers, Foppen is unresolved, and management's own incentive range tops out at 8 percent EPS growth.

A staircase of dated steps would move Hilton from turning up to broadening, and three of those steps, all in 2027, are the decisive tests. Three of the steps would be new information for the market: a Foppen outcome, Canada's first-year profit compared with the most cautious broker's forecast, and, further out, a second Walmart site or a share buyback.

A stall would take the multiple back to 9.5x to 10.5x, and a collapse would take it to 8x on lower earnings. A stall would follow a Canada slip past mid-2027 or a Canada first-half loss above £2m to £3m, negative West core-meat volumes, an Oceania margin below 3.0 percent, a Foppen write-off presented as trading, or a FY2027 range well below consensus followed by a September miss. A collapse would follow a core-contract event or a food-safety event in the core business.

Where I differ from the market. The share price says the thesis is broadening; the fundamentals say Hilton is turning up. The gap between the two is the 2027 test year, and the market is paying for that year in advance.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. I agree with the Analyst rather than the computed Broadening: the cause for concern has cleared and volumes and cash have turned, but continuing profit before tax fell 8.9% in H1 FY26, FY2026 is a like-for-like decline, FY2027 is flat with a probable consensus cut, and the growth engine (Canada) first shows in H2 FY27; the repair is priced (8.1x to the five-year median), so this is Turning up ten months in, with the next 6-12 months more likely to test than to broaden the thesis. Strong current momentum keeps it at the middle; just below Greggs' Bottoming/early Turning with profit beating, above BP's late Reinforcing at a commodity peak.

#11The fair multiple

Conclusion: the fair multiple for a turning-up Hilton is 12x to 14x two-year-forward earnings (the five-year median to the five-year 75th percentile), with 15x available in 2028 if Canada proves that the model still travels. The 20.64x guideline belongs to the pre-2022 compounder and should not be used for the return.

The dashboard's guideline multiple is 20.64x, which is 75 percent above today's multiple. The Phases page assigns Hilton to "Broadening" and so gives a guideline fair multiple of 20.64x two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history. The ten-year bands are 12.5x at the 10th percentile, 16.9x at the median, 19.8x at the 75th percentile and 22.9x at the 90th; the Phases page reads today's multiple as 11.79x.

My view: a fair multiple of 12x to 14x now, with a path to about 15x in 2028 if Canada proves that Hilton's model still travels. Five arguments support that view.

  • Hilton's ten-year valuation range describes two different companies. From 2016 to mid-2022 Hilton traded at 15x to 22x (share prices of 600p to 1,268p) as a compounder that followed grocers into Australia, Central Europe and the Nordics with a clean earnings record. Since September 2022, when the first warning took the multiple to 8.7x, the range has been 8.2x to 14.6x, with a median of about 11.9x, through two warnings, three failed adjacent businesses, a chief executive's exit and a de-rating to 8.1x. The 80th percentile of the whole decade describes the first company. Today's company is the second one: it has the same contract economics, but it has demonstrated a capacity to disappoint, and its margin has halved on FactSet's basis.
  • The business the market is valuing has no margin lever and modest growth. On our numbers, EPS grows 3.4 percent a year from FY2025 to FY2028, and about 8 to 9 percent a year from the FY2026 trough, of which 2 to 3 points come from the finance line. Management's stretch incentive target is 8 percent. A business that reinvests about a third of its cash flow at 15 to 20 percent pre-tax returns and pays out the rest supports a multiple near its five-year median. Such a business has upside to the five-year 75th percentile (13.8x) only if the reinvestment proves high-return, and proving that is Canada's job.
  • Peers set the ceiling for Hilton's multiple. Cranswick, the compounder standard, trades at 14.8x, its own 11th percentile; Greencore, the self-help precedent, trades at 9.4x, and LDC at 10.0x. A 20.64x multiple would put Hilton at a 40 percent premium to Cranswick with a quarter of Cranswick's margin. The ten-year "conservative" band (15.4x) is about Cranswick's multiple today. Hilton can reach 15.4x only when its growth is visibly contracted and its record is clean again, which is a question for 2028.
  • The phase argument points to the lower part of the range. Hilton is turning up, and its forecasts are more uncertain than usual (a ±13 percent range for FY2027 EPS and a probable consensus cut in April 2027). For such a stock the guideline's own logic says to use the lower part of the historical range, not the 80th percentile. "Broadening" is the dashboard's reading of price momentum, not of the thesis.
  • Hilton's multiple is driven by company news, not by the sector. Peers explain only 10 percent of the variance in Hilton's share price. The re-rating from 8.1x to 11.75x happened on company news, and the next moves will too. Hilton's valuation floor is therefore company-specific, and it has been tested: 8.1x, reached when the chief executive had gone.

Each view of the multiple implies a share price, on two-year-forward EPS of about 62p.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's target prices (720p to 850p, mean 795p) imply about 12x to 13.5x on the brokers' own forecasts, which is my range. The dashboard's guideline is the outlier, and the guideline is the figure that produces the model's +104 percent return.

What would move my view towards the guideline: Canada reaching £10m or more of operating profit by 2029 with a second site announced, Foppen resolved and the dividend covered twice by free cash flow. That combination would re-prove the 2010s formula, and 15x to 17x would then be defensible. What would move my view towards the trough: a FY2027 miss of the FY2025 kind.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. The raw readings give B (cheap on one, neutral on the other), but step 2 moves it to C: the ten-year range is mostly the pre-2022 compounder at 15-22x, while the business today has a halved margin, two warnings and a narrower perimeter, and on the five-year range (median 11.9x) today's 11.75x is neutral, so the cheapness against its own history is largely deserved. I place it at the top of C because the peer discount is real if small and the Analyst's fair 12-14x still sits above the price.

#12Total shareholder return, by the DuPont split

Conclusion: at the guideline multiple the return is +104 percent to December 2027, three-quarters of it from a multiple I cannot justify. At my fair 13x the return is about +32 percent to December 2027 and +52 percent to June 2029 (17 percent a year), roughly half from earnings, a third from the multiple and the rest from dividends. At an unchanged multiple the return is about 13 percent a year, which is the floor case if Hilton passes the 2027 tests.

The model's return at the guideline multiple is +104.4 percent to 31 December 2027 and +132.7 percent to 30 June 2029. The DuPont split breaks the return into three parts: the change in earnings and the change in the multiple multiply together, and dividends add to the result. The December 2027 date is the model's 18-month column, 14 months from today; at that date the model values each share at £14.85. The June 2029 date is the model's three-year column; the return to that date is 37 percent a year, and the model values each share at £16.91. At both dates the multiple moves from 11.7x to 20.64x (+75.7 percent).

Three-quarters of the model's return comes from the multiple, which rests on topic #11; the earnings part is modest and is the only part the research can defend. Earnings add 12 percent over 14 months and 25 percent over 32 months, because FY2027 is flat and the step-up comes in FY2028 to FY2030. The earnings part is the model's EPS of 62p in FY2028 and 69p in FY2029, measured against 62p of two-year-forward consensus EPS today; the Analyst's cross-check EPS (60.7p and 67.7p) would trim the earnings part by about 2 points. The dividend adds about 5 percent a year on the current 35p.

My return at my fair multiple of 13x, on the same earnings, is about +32 percent to December 2027 and about +52 percent to June 2029.

  • To December 2027: earnings +11.6 percent and the multiple +11 percent (11.7x to 13x) give a price rise of 24 percent; dividends add about 8 percent, for a total of about +32 percent, roughly 27 percent a year.
  • To June 2029: earnings +24.8 percent and the multiple +11 percent give a price rise of 39 percent; dividends add about 13 percent, for a total of about +52 percent, roughly 17 percent a year.
  • At 14x: add about 8 points to each figure.
  • At an unchanged 11.75x: about +20 percent to December 2027 and +38 percent to June 2029 (about 13 percent a year), almost all from earnings and dividends.
  • At a trough 9.5x: about -1 percent to December 2027 (earnings +11.6 percent times a multiple change of -19 percent, plus 8 percent of dividends) and about +14 percent to June 2029.
  • On the Analyst's cross-check EPS, each figure is about 2 to 3 points lower.

The shape of Hilton's return matters as much as its size: the dividend pays first, the multiple's risk comes in 2027, and the earnings arrive last. The earnings part adds almost nothing in the next twelve months and then 10 to 11 percent a year. The April and September 2027 results decide whether the multiple holds at 11.75x, rises towards 13x to 14x, or falls to 9.5x to 10.5x. The dividend is the one part of the return that pays while waiting, and the balance sheet funds it until strict free cash flow covers it in FY2028 (topic #6).

The options that sit outside all of these return figures lean to the upside but are undated; the downside events are rarer but larger per share.

Where I differ from the market. The sell-side's mean target price (795p) implies about +11 percent plus the dividend yield, about a 16 percent one-year return. My return at 13x is similar over 14 months and higher over three years, because I carry Canada and Poland ramping in FY2029 where the single FY2029 broker does not. Both returns are far below the model's guideline return, and both are modest for a stock that has just risen 60 percent.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. The memo's central return of about 28-32% lies in the 20-35% band, giving B, and the three-year return of about 17% a year confirms it; the +104% at the 20.64x guideline is rejected with the memo's reasoning. I place it a little below the 82 that 27-30% would earn because the lower tail is fat: an unchanged multiple gives about +20%, a stall to 9.5x about nil, the near-term revision skew is negative and trough earnings at a trough multiple sit 35% below the price.

#13Summary conclusion on the business and its investment case

Hilton Food is a durable, medium-quality contract packer whose repair is done and priced, and whose growth engine has been rebuilt but not yet restarted. Hilton has a real volume moat, no pricing power and a repair team that has done its job. Hilton's growth engine is dedicated plants in new countries under fixed-fee contracts. The shares have risen 60 percent from a distressed low to the five-year median multiple, which is the right price for a repaired business whose earnings are at a trough.

From here the case is a back-loaded earnings step-up of about a third by FY2030, paid for with a 4.9 percent yield. On the model, EPS rises from 57p to 76p. FY2027 is flat and probably brings a consensus cut; FY2028 to FY2030 then bring 10 to 11 percent annual growth from Canada, Poland, the removal of seafood losses and a falling finance charge.

The skew is slightly negative over the next 6 to 12 months, which is not the setup Richard looks for, but positive over 18 to 36 months. The longer-term positives are not in the price: Canada's contract terms, the Woolworths contract running to 2033, a capital return once leverage reaches its 1.0x floor, and a FY2029 consensus that only one broker has forecast.

The fair multiple is 12x to 14x, not the 20.64x guideline, and at 13x the return is about 17 percent a year to mid-2029, mostly from earnings and dividends.

Three dated tests decide the case in 2027. The January 2027 trading update should show Canada commissioned and Christmas volumes; the 7 April 2027 results should show FY2026 delivered in the upper half of guidance and set the first FY2027 range; and the September 2027 interim results will show whether H1 FY27 is flat, as in our base case, or growing, as consensus implies.

The risks that matter are sudden and geared. The sudden risks are a West stream re-allocated, a Canada slip and a food-safety event; the gearing comes from a 2 percent margin and a finance charge of 28 percent of operating profit. A fair trough price sits about 20 percent below today's price. If Hilton passes the 2027 tests, it becomes a broadening case in 2028 with a path to 15x; if Hilton fails the September test, the stock stalls at 9.5x to 10.5x, with the dividend as the cushion.

The four memo ratings are graded against other listed European companies: A is the top 10 percent, B the next 15 percent, C the next 25 percent, D the next 25 percent and F the bottom 25 percent.

End notes

Price and date. The memo was written on 3 November 2026 at 715.5p, the dashboard close of 29 October 2026; the Financial Analyst's model used 726p, the close of 28 October 2026. Market capitalisation is about £650m.

Definitions. "Operating profit" is the company's adjusted operating profit on today's continuing perimeter, which excludes the sold Fairfax Meadow, Foods Connected and Dalco businesses. EPS is the company's adjusted EPS. Money is in pounds sterling and per-share figures are in pence.

Consensus. Consensus is the FactSet median of 28 October 2026. Three brokers are visible by name: Deutsche Bank, Peel Hunt and Shore Capital.

Forecasts. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst's model after update 2 (EPS of 57p, 56p, 62p, 69p and 76p for FY2026 to FY2030). The Analyst's own cross-check deducts about £1m of minorities and carries a slightly higher finance charge, giving EPS of 54.0p, 55.1p, 60.7p, 67.7p and 74.1p. Where the memo gives sensitivities, it uses the cross-check's building blocks, because those are the figures that reconcile to the company's accounts.

Names and abbreviations. Viewforth is the house view. NADEC is Hilton's Saudi Arabian joint-venture partner. MLA is Meat & Livestock Australia; the CMA is the UK Competition and Markets Authority; the FDA is the United States Food and Drug Administration. IFRS 16 and IFRS 18 are international accounting standards for leases and for the presentation of the income statement.

Grades. A 90 to 100, B 75 to 89, C 50 to 74, D 25 to 49, F 1 to 24; each topic's score is set by the Rater.

Visuals and tables. Colours in the charts: history blue, consensus violet, Viewforth orange, peers aqua; red marks falls and risks. Charts drawn for this page take their figures from the memo. Default visuals and Richard's five financial tables (annual history, recent periods, FactSet consensus, broker detail and segments) come from FactSet, the Master Dashboard and the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst's model (update 2); each figure's note gives its basis.

Basis. History in the default visuals is on FactSet's reported basis, while the memo's operating profit and EPS are the company's adjusted figures on today's continuing perimeter, so the two can differ.
